key_facts: **Paronychia** is inflammation of the nail fold: **acute** (usually bacterial, hours–days) or **chronic** (over about 6 weeks).
Acute: *S. aureus* or streptococci after minor trauma; one digit; pain, redness, pus.
Chronic: **wet work** destroys the cuticle; irritant dermatitis of the fold with *Candida* colonisation; several fingers.
Acute: warm soaks, drain pus; antibiotics only if spreading, unwell or high risk. Chronic: keep hands dry, cotton-lined gloves, potent steroid to the fold ± azole.
Grouped vesicles: **herpetic whitlow**, do not incise. A single persistent 'paronychia' may be melanoma or SCC.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Paronychia** = inflammation of the proximal and/or lateral nail folds. **Acute** (<~6 weeks) is usually bacterial (*S. aureus*, streptococci, sometimes *Pseudomonas*) or herpetic whitlow; **chronic** (>~6 weeks) is often related to irritant dermatitis of the nail fold plus secondary **Candida** (and sometimes Gram-negative bacteria).

**Candidal nail disease** usually follows chronic paronychia: yeast involves the fold first, then may spread to the nail plate (onychomycosis / onycholysis). Typical case: **candidal onychomycosis with paronychia** in a wet-work hairdresser with KOH yeast cells.

sub: Acute: any age, nail-biters, manicures, children sucking fingers.
Chronic: wet-work occupations (hairdressers, cleaners, caterers, healthcare), diabetes.

ul: Repeated **wet work**, cold hands, manicure trauma, cuticle picking, and irritants lift/lose the cuticle → gap between fold and plate → colonisation by *Candida albicans* (± bacteria).
Occupations: hairdressers, cleaners, bartenders, food handlers, dairy/fishing, home wet work.
Host factors: hand dermatitis, diabetes, immunosuppression, poor peripheral circulation.

Candida nail-plate infection is **less common** than dermatophyte onychomycosis overall, and is relatively **more often fingernails** than toenails. Relevance of a positive Candida culture must be judged clinically (Candida can secondarily colonise dystrophic nails from psoriasis/trauma).
Breach of the cuticle seal between fold and nail plate.
**"Chronic paronychia is a fungal infection"**: it is mainly irritant dermatitis of the fold; *Candida* is secondary.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: The **cuticle** is the seal; once it is lost, irritants and microbes get under the fold.

mech.t: Trauma, picking, manicures or wet work break the cuticle seal.
Bacteria enter the fold, forming pus beneath the eponychium.

mech.t: Repeated wetting causes irritant dermatitis; the fold lifts from the plate and *Candida* and Gram-negative bacteria colonise the gap.

sections.title: Clinical features

head: Feature
Typical findings
rows: Swollen, tender, erythematous proximal (± lateral) folds; **loss of cuticle**; fold lifted off plate; intermittent white/yellow/green discharge
Thickening, yellow/white/green/black discolouration, **transverse ridging**, onycholysis starting near the fold
Fingers (thumbs common); often **several** digits over time; wet-work hands
Hairdresser; 6 months yellow thumbnails; painful cuticles; yellow malodorous secretion; onycholysis; KOH **yeast**

ul: Clinical: chronicity, wet-work history, cuticle loss, multi-digit tendency, discharge.

sections.title: Management

ul: Keep hands **dry and warm**; cotton-lined waterproof gloves for wet work; change when damp.
Avoid cuticle cutting/picking and harsh manicures.
Emollient barrier frequently; trim nails short.
Occupational advice for hairdressers: PPE, dry between clients, treat hand dermatitis.

blocks: **Drug therapy (align with BNF/local formulary; confirm organism when possible):**

ul: Chronic paronychia: treat **dermatitis of the fold** (short courses of topical corticosteroid ointment to the fold are often used in specialist pathways) **plus** topical antifungal/antiseptic solutions to the nail fold for weeks–months (e.g. imidazole solutions — check BNF).

Confirmed Candida nail/fold disease not settling: oral **itraconazole** or **fluconazole** (Candida-active). **Itraconazole** is usually preferred (broader spectrum vs Candida than terbinafine; fingernail regimens often ~6 weeks continuous or pulsed per product licence — **verify current BNF/SmPC**).
**Terbinafine** is first-line for many **dermatophyte** nail infections but is **less reliable** for Candida — do not default to it when yeast is the culprit.
Topical nail lacquers alone are often insufficient if matrix/proximal disease or significant fold infection.
Abscess: drainage pathway; antibiotics only when bacterial infection is clear.

blocks: **If no improvement after appropriate oral course:** revisit adherence, ongoing wet exposure, alternative diagnoses (psoriasis, trauma), re-mycology, and dermatology referral.

ul: **No abscess:** **warm water (± saline) soaks 3–4 times a day for 10–15 min**, keep the finger dry between soaks, rest/elevate, and give analgesia. Most cases settle without antibiotics.

**Abscess (fluctuant, pointing pus):** **incision and drainage** (or lifting the eponychium with a blade) in primary care, minor injuries or urgent care. Partial nail removal if pus has tracked under the plate. Antibiotics are often not needed after adequate drainage.

**Antibiotics only if** there is spreading cellulitis, the patient is systemically unwell, or they are immunocompromised or diabetic: **flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5–7 days**; **clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily** if penicillin-allergic (erythromycin in pregnancy); **co-amoxiclav** if from a finger-sucking child or a bite (anaerobes, *Eikenella*)

**Refer same day** for suspected **flexor tenosynovitis** (Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, flexed posture, tenderness along the sheath, pain on passive extension), **felon** (pulp-space abscess), osteomyelitis, or spreading infection in diabetes.

**Recurrent acute episodes** in the same fold should make you think of an underlying chronic paronychia, an ingrowing nail, HSV, or (single digit, persistent, in an older adult) **SCC of the nail unit or amelanotic melanoma**.

blocks: **Ingrowing toenail** is a separate problem: see [Ingrowing toenail](condition:ingrowing-toenail).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Spreading cellulitis, lymphangitis, fever or a **tense swollen finger pulp** (felon) or tendon-sheath signs: same-day surgical assessment.
Grouped vesicles on the finger: **herpetic whitlow**, so do not incise.
Diabetes, peripheral arterial disease or immunosuppression with a toe infection: low threshold for referral.
A single nail with persistent ‘paronychia’, nail destruction or pigment: exclude **nail-unit melanoma or SCC**.
Abscess, felon, flexor tenosynovitis, osteomyelitis.
Nail dystrophy; chronic disease lasting months.
Acute: settles in days with drainage. Chronic: months, and recurs unless wet work is controlled.

pearls: Treat the **fold environment**, not only the tablet — wet-work continuation is the common reason for “failed” antifungals.
Warn about itraconazole/fluconazole **interactions** (CYP3A4), LFTs, pregnancy/contraception issues — counsel and check interactions software.
Nails grow slowly: cosmetic improvement lags mycological cure by months.

rows: Chronic paronychia is caused by streptococci/*Pseudomonas*

**Chronic paronychia (>6 weeks)** is mainly an **irritant/eczematous** condition of the nail fold (wet work, cuticle loss) with **secondary *Candida* (± bacterial) colonisation**. Strep/staph cause **acute** paronychia, and *Pseudomonas* is a colonist (green nail). Treat with barrier repair: dry, gloves (cotton under rubber), emollient, **potent TCS ± topical azole** (CKS)
**Terbinafine is preferred for candidal paronychia/nail infection**

**Wrong for *Candida*.** Terbinafine is poorly active against yeasts and is the drug of choice for **dermatophyte** onychomycosis. *Candida* nail disease uses **itraconazole** pulses (or fluconazole off-label). Candidal paronychia without plate involvement uses a **topical azole ± TCS**
